## 4B.3 CARPORTS AND GARAGES


## Further controls that may apply:

SECTION C

PART 22 -  General Access and Parking


## Objectives


## Controls

- 1 To encourage the design of functional car parking facilities that are integrated with the built form of the dwelling.
- 2 Carports and garages are to present as complementary and sympathetic visual elements within the streetscape.
- 3 To ensure the garages and carports are not the primary built form when viewing the dwelling from the street or public domain.
- 4 To ensure the location of carports and garages considers existing trees, structures on adjacent sites, streetscape and visual character.
- 5 To minimise impacts of excavation on the built environment and the streetscape.
- 6 To minimise 3 storey streetscape building appearances in low density residential areas.
- 7 To avoid excavation in the front setback area and maintain existing ground levels to the street.

## Design of Carports and Garages

- 1 The car parking spaces, whether covered or uncovered, are to be located at or behind the required front setback as specified in Part 4A.2(2) & (15) of this DCP, or behind the front building line defined by the existing dwelling where the dwelling is being retained, whichever is the lesser.
- 2 The scale and design of carport and garage structures are:
- to be sympathetic to existing development on-site;
- ii) to consider adjacent buildings;
- iii) to consider proximity to drainage systems;
- iv) to be integrated into the building design; and
- not to dominate the site, dwelling and landscape, or the streetscape.
- 3 Alterations and additions should not prevent the future ability of the site to accommodate two car spaces behind the building line.
- 4 Council may consider a reduced setback for parking spaces on steeply sloping sites.
- 5 Where it is not possible to locate the parking structure space behind the minimum permissible setback or the building line due to topographical constraints or side setback space of less than 3m, structure is to comply with the following:
- the structure is to be open sided;
- ii) the structure is to be located at the maximum possible distance from the front property boundary; and
- iii) the design of the structure is be of a scale and form that is compatible with the streetscape character.
- 6 The width of any detached or attached carport/garage visible from the street is not to be greater than 6m, as measured to the outer face of the exterior walls/column/posts (refer to Fig 4B.3-1).
- 7 Basement garages are only permitted on sloping land and where no more than 1m excavation is required for driveway access.
![page 18 img 2 (244x44)](images/ku-ring-gai-development-control-plan/p0002-2a9e29032aaa.png)


<!-- SRC: 06-part-4-dwelling-houses.pdf | PAGE: 19 -->


## 4B.3 CARPORTS AND GARAGES (continued)


*Figure 4B.3-1- Maximum widths of garages and carports*


## Location of Parking Structures

- 8 Location of all new driveways and services are to enable preservation of existing site or street trees to which Part 13 of this DCP applies.
- 9 Where a site has a frontage to more than one road and/or service lane, access is to be obtained from:
- the road or service lane that is lower on the road hierarchy, and/ or
- ii) the road or service lane that carries the lower volume of traffic.
Note: Road hierarchy and traffic volumes will be determined by Council at its discretion.


## Detached Carports and Garages

- 10 Detached garages are to be single storey and set back 1.5m minimum from side and rear boundaries.
- 11 Detached carports are to be single storey and set back 0.6m minimum from side and rear boundaries.
Note: Where there is any inconsistency between this Part and Part 22 of this DCP in relation to vehicular access, car parking or garages, this section prevails to the extent of the inconsistency.

## 4C.1 BUILDING ENVELOPES


## Further controls that may apply:


## Objectives


## Controls

- 1 To limit the height and bulk of buildings so that they do not dominate the natural landscape or the tree canopy.
- 2 To ensure that buildings are responsive to the site.
- 3 To maintain the integrity of the existing streetscape.
- 4 To provide for quality interior spaces while considering the external building form requirements.
- 5 To limit the extent of visual and noise intrusion on the private spaces of neighbouring properties.
- 6 To allow adequate daylight, sunlight and ventilation to habitable rooms and private open spaces for new and neighbouring dwellings of the site and of neighbouring sites.
- 7 To ensure that significant views from neighbouring dwellings and public reserves are not adversely impacted.
- 1 The maximum height of a dwelling is 9.5m (including any garage, basement or the like) and present as a 2 storey dwelling house as illustrated in Figure 4C.1-1
![page 22 img 2 (244x44)](images/ku-ring-gai-development-control-plan/p0002-2a9e29032aaa.png)

Note: Standards (in metres) for the external height of the building are set within KLEP.


*Figure 4C.1-1: Maximum height of dwelling*

- 2 The following matters are to be considered with regard to the potential impact on neighbouring properties and local character:
- opportunities to minimise overshadowing of living and private open space areas and solar panels;
- ii) opportunities to minimise overlooking of living and private open space areas;
- iii) opportunities to minimise adverse impacts on any significant bushland, or distant views;
- iv) the relationship with the streetscape.
- 3 Development is to avoid the creation of an overbearing effect upon adjoining development by:
- ensuring appropriate side setbacks and landscaping are incorporated in the design;
- ii) ensuring all built structures are within the building height plane as illustrated in Figure 4C.1-2;
- iii) the relationship with the streetscape.

- 8 To minimise 3 storey streetscape building appearances and maintain a low density domestic scale in residential areas.
- 9 To avoid excavation outside the building line and ensure deep soil provision.
- 4 Basements are to be:
- consolidated under the building footprint.
- ii) minimised and no habitable spaces are permitted;
- iii) include a maximum ceiling height of 2.2m to all non-habitable rooms.

## 4C.2 BUILDING FACADES


## Further controls that may apply:

SECTION B

PART 20 -  Development Near Road or Rail Noise SECTION C

PART 23.3

-  Sustainability of Building Materials


## Controls

- 1 Extensive blank or unarticulated walls to street frontages will not be permitted.
- 2 All external facades are to be articulated to reduce the apparent building mass and present a human scale. This may be achieved through the use of bay window openings, window awnings, chimney and alcove features, verandas, pergolas, balconies, entry porches, staggered wall planes, a combination of materials and finishes, decorative architectural elements including brick corbelling, banding and recesses.
- 3 The maximum length for an unrelieved wall is 12m. Where walls exceed 4m in height, the maximum length for an unrelieved wall is 8m.
- 4 Side elevations are to avoid unrelieved walls. This may be achieved by:
- dividing walls into sections, bays or modules;
- ii) separating wall sections with recesses or courtyards.
![page 24 img 2 (244x44)](images/ku-ring-gai-development-control-plan/p0002-2a9e29032aaa.png)


## Objectives

- 1 To encourage well designed, attractive and site responsive buildings.
- 2 To minimise the bulk and scale of the built form.
- 3 To avoid massive and unrelieved walls to side boundaries

<!-- SRC: 06-part-4-dwelling-houses.pdf | PAGE: 25 -->


## Objectives

- 4 To ensure the integration of alterations and additions into an existing building so that the building continues to appear as a single dwelling.
- 5 To ensure high impact elements such as noise sources are considered early in the design stage.

## 4C.2 BUILDING FACADES (continued)


## Controls

- 5 Alterations and additions to an existing dwelling are to be:
- designed so that they are integrated into the existing building;
- ii) result in the new and old structures appearing as one building from the street. This may be achieved through the choice of materials, detailing, building proportion and configuration.
- 6 Building design is to integrate soft landscaping and natural site features and make provision for tall shrub plantings.
- 7 Where dwellings are located near a busy road or railway line, the requirements of Part 20.1 of this DCP are to be included.

## Corner Sites

- 8 Corner sites are to address both primary and secondary street frontages using building and landscaping elements such as feature windows, or other treatments to wall surfaces.
Note:

Refer t o 4A.1 (5-6) and 4A.2 of this Part.

## Objectives

- 1 To integrate the first floor of dwellings into the design of the development.
- 2 To avoid an overbearing bulk and scale relationship with neighbouring properties, particularly on sloping sites.
- 3 To allow adequate daylight, sunlight and ventilation to living area and private open spaces of new and neighbouring dwellings.
- 4 To encourage view sharing.
- 5  To encourage use of attic rooms within the roof space for habitable purposes as an alternative to a second storey, particularly in neighbourhoods that are predominantly single storey dwellings.
![page 26 img 2 (244x44)](images/ku-ring-gai-development-control-plan/p0002-2a9e29032aaa.png)


## 4C.3 FIRST FLOOR DESIGN AND ROOF FORMS


## Controls


## First Floor Design

- 1 Dwelling design is to avoid an overbearing bulk/scale relationship with neighbouring properties. Consideration is to be given to avoiding large vertical wall surfaces by stepping back upper levels and containing within the existing/proposed roof space.
- 2 The placement of windows in first floor walls facing side boundaries are to respect the privacy of neighbouring properties.

## Attic Rooms

- 3 Attic room designs are to avoid:
- increasing the bulk of the building;
- ii) causing undue overshadowing of adjacent properties and open spaces;
- iii) causing loss of significant views from adjacent properties; or
- iv) being excessive in scale and bulk relative to the rest of the building.
- 4 The form and placement of any windows is to respect the privacy of neighbouring properties.
- 5 Attic rooms are to be located within the existing roof forms and retain the streetscape appearance of the existing buildings. In some cases depending on location of building and shape of roof, higher roof forms for attics may be considered.

## Roof Line

- 6 Roof structures are to be designed to minimise bulk and overshadowing of neighbouring buildings and open spaces by:
- considered selection of material, colour and pitch;
- ii) use of low-angled pitched roofs providing that they are compatible with existing development and the streetscape character; or
- iii) inclusion of habitable rooms within the roof space.

## Gables

- 7 Unless otherwise consistent with the form of development within the immediate locality, gables are:
- to be positioned a minimum of 0.2m below the main roof ridge height;
- ii) not to occupy any more than 40% of the face of any gable wall and not occupy more than 20% of the face of any roof or slope for a gable window;
- iii) not extend beyond the external wall of the dwelling.

<!-- SRC: 06-part-4-dwelling-houses.pdf | PAGE: 27 -->


## 4C.3 FIRST FLOOR DESIGN AND ROOF FORMS (continued)


## Controls


## Dormers

- 8 Dormer windows are to be located and have a size, bulk and scale that do not dominate the roof form or add excessively to the bulk of the building.
- 9 Dormer windows may only be provided on buildings with an architectural character or style that is suitable for dormer features.
- 10 Unless otherwise consistent with the form of development within the immediate locality, the configuration of dormer windows must satisfy the following:
- be positioned a minimum of 0.2m below the main roof ridge height;
- ii) not to extend beyond the external wall of the dwelling;
- iii) be set back from the sides of the roof by a minimum of 500mm.
- 11 Dormers occurring in the same roof plane must be similarly sized and configured, and arranged symmetrically.

## Clerestory Windows and Skylights

- 12 The location, size, configuration and layout of clerestory windows and skylights must be sympathetic to the overall design of the dwelling and the streetscape.

*Figure 4C.3-1 Clerestory window and skylight*


## Mechanical Equipment

- 13 Plant and equipment is to be integrated into the overall design of the roof and be contained within the roof form or screened behind parapet walls. These elements include lift overruns, plant equipment and air conditioning.

## 4C.4 PRIVATE OPEN SPACE

| Further controls that may apply:   | Further controls that may apply:                                          |
|------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------|
|                                    | SECTION C PART 21.2 - Landscape Design PART 23.8 - General Visual Privacy |


## Objectives

- 1 To ensure development proposals provide useable private open spaces as part of the overall design.

## Controls

- 1 At least one area of useable private open space which has a minimum depth of 5m and a minimum area of 50m 2 is to be provided on each site. On steep sites Council may consider a reduction in the minimum depth requirement.
- 2 On constrained sites (biodiversity, riparian, steep topography) Council may consider decks as open space.
- 3 Landscape areas are to provide functional outdoor areas that:
- are useable and relate well to indoor living areas;
- ii) have a character that is consistent with or enhances the landscape character of the area;
- iii) are located in consideration of noise, temperature, shade and screening;
- iv) are not dominated by adjoining development (in terms of overshadowing and overlooking);
- 4 Private open space is to constitute at least one north facing area providing adequate solar access. Refer to 4C.5 of this Part.
![page 28 img 2 (244x44)](images/ku-ring-gai-development-control-plan/p0002-2a9e29032aaa.png)


<!-- SRC: 06-part-4-dwelling-houses.pdf | PAGE: 29 -->


## Objectives

- 1 To ensure the design and siting of new development maintains a reasonable level of daylight and sunlight to habitable rooms, private open space, and solar collectors of new and neighbouring development.

## 4C.5 SOLAR ACCESS


## Controls

- 1 Solar access to habitable areas, private open space and solar collectors on the site and on neighbouring sites is to be preserved by:
- consideration of siting and orientation of buildings;
- ii) use of setbacks which increase with building heights;
- iii) landscape design and location of vegetation including deciduous or tall trees;
- iv) consideration of window locations and size.
- 2 A building is to be designed and sited to maintain solar access to adjoining properties of at least 4 hours between 9am and 3pm on 21 st June to north facing windows and all living areas (family rooms, rumpus, lounge and kitchen) and the principal private open space recreational areas, such as swimming pools and patios.
- 3 Dwelling design and orientation is to provide at least 4 hours between 9am and 3pm on 21 st June to north facing windows and all living areas (family rooms, rumpus, lounge and kitchen) and the principal private open space including swimming pools and patios, to the proposed dwelling.
- 4 Where shadows cast by existing buildings preclude satisfying the above requirements, sunlight during winter solstice (21 st June) should not be reduced by more than 20%.
- 5 Development is to consider the use of sun protection devices that preserve internal amenity. These can include window shades and awnings, roof and eave overhangs, use of pergolas and landscaping for shading of openings.
- 6 Professionally prepared Shadow Diagrams must accompany all applications for new dwellings and alterations/additions exceeding one storey. Refer to Council's DA Guide.
Note: See Council's website for DA guide at www.krg.nsw.gov.au


<!-- SRC: 06-part-4-dwelling-houses.pdf | PAGE: 30 -->

![page 30 img 1 (195x51)](images/ku-ring-gai-development-control-plan/p0002-b2bfe3c5fb15.png)


## Objectives

- 1 To ensure a high level of internal amenity for all occupants with direct access to fresh air for all habitable rooms.
- 2 To create a breeze path to let in fresh air and flush out stale air.
- 3 To enable areas of the dwelling to be closed off to reduce areas requiring heating and cooling.
![page 30 img 2 (244x44)](images/ku-ring-gai-development-control-plan/p0002-2a9e29032aaa.png)


## 4C.6 NATURAL VENTILATION


## Controls

- 1 Building design is to incorporate measures for natural cross ventilation. This may be achieved by:
- locating openings such as windows, sky lights, doors in opposite walls;
- ii) include open plan living areas;
- iii) include doors that can section off heating and cooling living areas;
- iv) include vents above or in internal doors to facilitate cross ventilation;
- elevate the house so that air can circulate beneath it;
- vi) positioning of opening to control air flow, for example, use clerestory windows, rood ventilators and vents in ridges, eaves and ceilings to create convection currents; and
- vii) carports and garages should be placed so that they do not block ventilation into the house .

- 1 To ensure that ancillary facilities are integrated into the landscape and are unobtrusive to neighbours and the public domain.
- 2 To ensure ancillary facilities are adequate, and well designed and located.
- 3 To ensure reasonable provision is made on site and within the site plan for the provision of ancillary facilities.
- 4 To prevent access to pool areas other than through the gate.

## Swimming Pools, Spas, Equipment & Fences

- 1 The swimming pool/spa and/or enclosure is to consider the location, design, finish and colour to minimise the impact on the landform when viewed from adjacent public domain and private property.
- 2 The swimming pool/spa and/or enclosure is to be designed and located so that there is sufficient area adjacent to the property boundary for substantial landscape planting to:
- minimise potentially adverse impacts such as glare, and visual intrusion;
- ii) minimise the impact on existing trees both on site and on adjoining properties.
- 3 The swimming pool/spa coping, decking, paving or the like is to be sited a minimum of 2m from a property boundary and not be more than 0.5m above existing ground level at any point. On steeply sloping sites, levels greater than 0.5m will be considered subject to increased setbacks and landscaping to protect the amenity and privacy of neighbouring properties.
Note: Refer to AS 1926 Swimming Pool Safety for requirements on pool fencing and landscaping to Non-Climbable Zones.

- 4 Pool excavation should not be beneath the canopy of trees protected by Part 13 of this DCP.
- 5 The swimming pool/spa is to be sited and designed to ensure that pool waters do not discharge to stormwater drains, natural waterways, natural bushland, or neighbouring private property by using the following methods:
- connecting backwash to the sewer;
- ii) installing a surface drain to collect overflow stormwater; or
- iii) ensure the immediate pool surrounds slope toward the pool; or
- iv) other acceptable design solutions approved by Council.
Note: Refer Part 24D.7 Swimming Pools and Spas of this DCP.

 Note: Refer to Council's Policy Swimming Pool Safety (new pools or existing pools).

## Objectives

- 5 To ensure tennis courts are located with sufficient area between the court and the property boundary to:
- Minimise adverse impacts such as noise, overlooking and visual intrusion.
- ii) Provide sufficient area for appropriate landscaping.
- iii) Minimise impacts to existing trees.

## 4C.7 ANCILLARY FACILITIES (continued)


## Controls

- 6 All mechanical equipment, including filters, pumps and heaters associated with the swimming pool and/or spa are housed within an enclosure. The enclosure is to be sound-proofed to the extent that noise from the operation of the mechanical equipment does not exceed 5dB(A) above the background noise (LA90, 15 min) level during the day when measured at the boundary of the nearest potentially affected residential occupancies and is not audible in habitable rooms of any residences at night (from 8.00pm to 7.00am). The background (LA90, 15 min) level is to be determined without the noise source present.
![page 32 img 2 (252x44)](images/ku-ring-gai-development-control-plan/p0032-f78b5107e4a2.png)


*Figure 4C.7-1: Swimming pool controls.*


## Tennis Courts

- 7 Tennis courts are to be located at the rear of properties. For corner allotments, or where the property has two street frontages, the location of tennis court is not to be in the primary frontage.
- 8 Noise and overlooking to neighbouring properties is to be minimised by:
- ensuring a distance of at least 3m between the court and the property boundary;
- ii) ensuring the finished tennis court level is not more than 1m above existing ground level at any point; and
- iii) planting trees and tall shrubs between the tennis court and the property boundary.
- 9 On steeply sloping sites, tennis courts with a finished court level higher than 1m above existing ground level will be considered subject to increased setbacks and landscaping to protect the amenity and privacy of neighbouring properties.
- 10 The increase of runoff associated with tennis courts is to be avoided by ensuring that an on-site stormwater detention system is provided, and utilising WSUD and filtration pits.
![page 32 img 3 (276x189)](images/ku-ring-gai-development-control-plan/p0032-40618927d253.png)

Objectives

- 6 To maintain amenity of surrounding properties in terms of noise, particularly at night.
- 7 To ensure outbuildings and utility areas are sympathetically positioned on the site and do not detract from the visual quality of the area.

## 4C.7 ANCILLARY FACILITIES (continued)


## Controls

- 11 Earthworks associated with the construction of a tennis court are not to unreasonably alter the natural topography of the land or alter the natural groundwater table. (Refer to Part 21.1 Earthworks and Slope of this DCP.)
- 12 The materials used in the construction of a tennis court, including the type and colour of court surfaces, are to be carefully selected to complement natural bushlands and any adjacent Heritage Item.
- 13 Tennis courts are to be sited having regard to the location of habitable rooms both on-site and on adjoining properties, and to the maintenance of appropriate private open space areas. This is to be achieved by maintaining a minimum distance of 5m between the tennis court fence boundary and habitable rooms of any dwelling.
- 14 Lighting of tennis courts for night tennis will not be permitted.
- 15 Tennis hit-up walls will not be permitted.
- 16 The tennis court is to be sited to minimise the visual impact of the structure when viewed from the adjacent public domain and private property, and minimise the impact on the landform.
- 17 Conversions of grass tennis courts to impervious surfaces are to consider impact to built-upon area, water management and existing trees.
Note:

Refer to Council's Tennis Court Policy


## Outbuildings

- 18 Outbuildings including studios, hobby rooms, storage structures, cubby houses or cabanas, are to be located on the site having regard to the relationship with existing development on-site and on adjoining properties.
- 19 Consideration is to be given to the position of windows associated with habitable rooms and the potential impact of noise, fumes, loss of light, and ventilation.
- 20 Out-buildings are not to exceed a single storey. All out-buildings will be included in both floor space ratio calculations and built upon area calculations.
- 21 A minimum setback of 2m from boundaries is to apply for any outbuilding with a wall height exceeding 2m relative to the ground level at the boundary.
Note:

For detached garages see part 4B.3

- 1 Front fences are to maintain the streetscape character by being consistent with the established pattern of fences.

## 4C.8 FENCING


## Controls


## Front Fences

- 1 Fences are to:
- restrict visually solid forms (such as masonry, lapped and capped timber or brushwood) to 0.9m in height above existing ground level;
- ii) restrict the height of visually transparent fences (such as metal grille or timber picket) to 1.2m, (a transparent fence has an open to solid ratio of not less than 1:3).
- 2 Front fences in excess of 1.2m will only be permitted in areas where they are compatible and consistent with the streetscape. All such fences are to be set back at least 1m from the street boundary with provision of low maintenance screen planting in the setback area.
- 3 Front fencing is not encouraged in areas where it does not form part of the overall streetscape. In such areas, the front boundary can be defined by low hob walls, by garden beds or planting.
- 4 Front fencing is to enable outlook from dwellings to the street for safety and surveillance and should be generally low and visually permeable.
- 5 Shrub plantings on boundaries are desirable; however, hedges along the entire front boundary are to be no higher than the allowable fence height.
- 6 The footings of a fence within the Tree Protection Zone of a tree are not to adversely affect the health of the tree.

## 4C.8 FENCING (continued)


## Controls


## Side and rear fences

- 7 Side fences forward of the front building line are to be unobtrusive and allow for continuity of landscape vista between adjoining properties. Where this character predominates it must be respected in new developments.
- 8 Side fences on corner sites are to be designed and located so as to:
- maintain the streetscape character;
- ii) be consistent with the established pattern of fences;
- iii) ensure an adequate amount of useable private open space; and
- 9 Side fences forward of the front building line should be compatible with the established front fencing in the street.
Note: The provisions of the Dividing Fences Act 1991 also apply.

Note: Common boundary fencing proposals require the consent of the adjoining land owner.

- 10 The footings of a fence within the structural root zone of a tree are not to adversely affect the health of the tree.

## Fences adjoining bushland

- 11 Fences adjoining bushland should protect the bushland from domestic animals, blend harmoniously with the bushland setting, and allow movement of small fauna species where appropriate.

## Objectives

- 1 To enable efficient, effective and sustainable waste management practices.
- 2 To ensure waste collection and storage within the site that does not affect the amenity of residents with regard to odour, visual appearance or noise disturbance.
- 3 To ensure waste and recycling storage areas are designed and constructed to meet the requirements of the building's use and its occupants.
- 4 To ensure design and management of waste and recycling facilities protect public health and the local environment.
- 5 To ensure the design of the development incorporates effective waste minimisation principle.

## Controls


## General

- 1 During the design of the development, construction waste is to be minimised by:
- using recycled materials, selecting materials that reduce waste or do not require disposal, or can be reused or recycled in the future;
- ii) designing with minimal site disturbance by avoiding unnecessary excavation or fill.
- 2 Council's standard waste and recycling service is:
- 3 Developments is to allocate, within each property boundary, an area for storing Council specified waste and recycling bins, preferably located at the rear of the premises to minimise visual clutter. The storage area is to be a minimum of 3m from openable windows and integrated with the landscaping. Refer to 23R.5 of this Part for bin characteristics.
- 4 An on-site area for composting of green and food waste is to be allocated and indicated in the development application plan.

## 4C.10 MATERIALS AND FINISHES


## Further controls that may apply:

| SECTION C PART 23.3 -  Sustainability of Building Materials   |
|----------------------------------------------------------------|


## Objectives

- 1 To reflect and reinforce the local character of Ku-ring-gai.
- 2 To complement the streetscape and natural environment.
- 3 To promote the use of high quality materials, finishes and colours for building facade articulation design and visual interest.
- 4 To ensure the use of materials, finishes and colours creates well proportioned facades and minimises the visual bulk.
- 5 To encourage the use of a subdued palette of colours and limited range of hues for building consistency across the LGA.

## Controls

- 1 External walls must be constructed of high quality and durable materials and finishes.
Note: Material and finishes selection is to be made in accordance with objectives and controls as stated in Part 23.4 of this DCP to ensure low environmental impact.

- 2 Reuse or recycling of existing local materials such as sandstone and brick is encouraged.
- 3 Large, unbroken expanses of any single material and finish (rendered or not) to building facades must be avoided.
Note: Refer to Parts 6-10 of this DCP for relevant building facade articulation controls.

- 4 New development is to avoid extensive use of highly reflective or gloss materials on the exterior of buildings.
- 5 The exterior finish material (e.g. sandstone or brick) must be integral to the overall building façade design and must not appear to be cosmetic.
- 6 Where louvres are used, they are to be an integral element in the building façade design.
- 7 Where additions and alterations are proposed, external materials and finishes must complement the existing building.

## Colours

- 8 The selection of a colour scheme for new development and in the restoration of existing facades is to comply with the following guidelines:
- base colours for major areas of building façade are to be light in tone (e.g. earth tone) with minimal colour intensity (or hue) e.g. off white or grey colours. Larger expanses of bold colour, black and white must be avoided, as these detract from the prominence of other façade details. Contrasting tints, tones and shades are to be restricted to small areas.
- ii) highlight colours to window and door mouldings, string courses, parapet details and the like, are to be in sufficient contrast to the base colour. Strong colours to large sections of the building must be avoided. Details should be finished in a matt to semi-gloss range.
- 9 Natural earth tones are to be used on building facades in close proximity to bushland.

## INTRODUCTION

Secondary dwellings provide for an alternate housing choice within the Ku-ring-gai region.

This housing type caters for changing population demographics, particularly extended families, ageing parents and older children remaining at home. Secondary dwellings also give families the opportunity to use the accommodation as a source of secondary income in a changing economy. Secondary dwellings will provide an affordable housing type that is compatible with the surrounding residential character.

This Part provides guidance for development of secondary dwellings to meet the aims and objectives within the KLEP. It aims to provide a high residential amenity for occupants of secondary dwellings, while protecting the amenity of occupants of principal dwellings and neighbouring dwellings. All secondary dwellings are to be integrated into the existing single dwelling neighbourhood character through their location and appearance, and are required to be sympathetic to the principal dwelling in design and materials.

The contents within this Part do not, in any way, alter the need for the principal dwelling to comply with Part 4 Dwelling Houses .

## Objectives

- 1 To ensure that secondary dwellings preserve the amenity and liveability of the principal and neighbouring dwellings.
- 2 To maintain the character of the streetscape.
- 3 To ensure the secondary dwelling does not confuse the interpretation of a heritage place.
![page 4 img 2 (624x196)](images/ku-ring-gai-development-control-plan/p0002-f1c9b0ac33c3.png)


## Controls

- 1 Only one principal dwelling and one secondary dwelling is permitted in a single lot.
- 2 The installation of a secondary dwelling is not to compromise the controls stated for the principal dwelling within Part 4 of this DCP. Parts 4A.3 and 4A.4 continue to apply to the site as a whole, and include all development on the site (the principal dwelling, secondary dwelling and any ancillary development).
- 3 All secondary dwellings are to be of a single level whether they are detached, integrated with the principal dwelling, or above an existing garage.
- 4 Where a secondary dwelling is proposed on a heritage property or in a Heritage Conservation Area it is to comply with the requirement of Part 19D.5 and Part 19 in general.
Note : All secondary dwelling developments are to comply with BASIX.

Note : All secondary dwelling developments are to comply with the stormwater requirements of the principal dwelling.

## 4.1C.1 SOLAR ACCESS


## Controls

- 1 All habitable rooms of secondary dwellings are to have a window. The use of skylights or highlight windows as the primary source of daylight and ventilation is prohibited.
- 2 The secondary dwelling is to achieve at least 3 hours solar access between 9am and 3pm on 21 st June to living areas and private open space unless no practicable alternative is available.
- 3 Secondary dwellings are to maintain at least 3 hours solar access between 9am and 3pm on the 21 st June to the living spaces and private open spaces of the principal dwelling.
- 4 Secondary dwellings are to maintain at least 4 hours solar access between 9am and 3pm on the 21 st June to the living spaces and private open spaces of the neighbouring dwellings.
- 5 Secondary dwellings are not to overshadow existing solar panels/ photovoltaic cells of the principal dwelling or neighbouring dwellings.
- 6 Where existing overshadowing by buildings is greater than that permitted in 5C.1(2-5) of this Part , sunlight is not to be reduced by more than 20%.

<!-- SRC: 07-part-4-1-secondary-dwellings.pdf | PAGE: 17 -->


## Objectives

- 1 To provide useable outdoor space to all secondary dwellings.
- 2 To retain adequate private open space for the principal dwelling.

## 4.1C.2 PRIVATE OPEN SPACE


## Controls

- 1 Private open space for the secondary dwelling is to lead directly off the internal living area.
- 2 A secondary dwelling at ground level is to have a minimum nominated useable private open space area of 25m 2 , with a minimum dimension of 3.0 metres. This area may be located within the secondary dwelling setbacks.
- 3 Freestanding walls or fencing are not to be used to separate or screen the private ground floor open space of a secondary dwelling. Landscaping may be used as a screening device.
- 4 A secondary dwelling on the first floor level is to have an allocated private open space such as a balcony or terrace that is accessible directly from the living area. The minimum provision is indicated in the table below:
- 5 Where a first floor secondary dwelling proposal demonstrates that it is unable to provide private open space upon the first floor, Council may consider provision of that space at the ground level in line with 5C.2 (2) of this Part , at a location directly visible from the first floor living area of the secondary dwelling.
- 6 Private open space is to be orientated to receive a minimum 3 hours of solar access between 9am and 3pm on 21 st June where practicable.
| Type       | Minimum Balcony/ Terrace Requirement   | Minimum Dimension Requirement   |
|------------|----------------------------------------|---------------------------------|
| Studio     | 8m 2                                   | 2.4m                            |
| 1 bedroom  | 10m 2                                  | 2.4m                            |
| 2 bedrooms | 12m 2                                  | 2.4m                            |

- 4 Floors, walls and doors that connect the secondary dwelling to the principal dwelling are to meet the noise transmission and insulation requirements of the BCA and AS 2107 (1987) .

## INTRODUCTION

This Part applies to development for dual occupancy dwellings and associated ancillary development.

Applications for semi-detached dwellings are to be considered under this Part. Semi-detached dwellings are largely similar to a dual occupancy in the form of two dwellings attached by a party wall and then subdivided to form two separate lots. All references to dual occupancy in this Part apply to semi-detached dwellings where relevant.

This Part guides dual occupancy and semi-detached development to be consistent with the aims and objectives of the KLEP 2015. This Part also guides dual occupancy development permitted under Schedule 1 of KLEP 2015.

The aims of this Part are as follows:

- Ensure development is in keeping with the prevailing Ku-ringgai character of buildings within a landscaped garden setting, including tall canopy trees, and is consistent with the built form and streetscape of the area.
- ii) Ensure each development has sufficient landscaping to contribute to the conservation and replenishment of Ku-ringgai's tree canopy, including locally occurring native tree species.
- iii) Ensure development within a Heritage Conservation Area or in the vicinity of a Heritage item conserves, protects and is consistent with the heritage character and values.
- iv) Minimise the impact of development on adjoining properties.
-  Protect and minimise the impact of development on the natural environment, including impacts on soil structure, water table and erosion from water runoff and limited water infiltration opportunities.
- vi)  Minimise the depletion of raw materials and non-renewable resources.
- vii) Ensure development addresses the needs of the current community without compromising the ability to meet the needs of future generations, including management of heat island effects.
- viii)  Encourage housing of the highest architectural, environmental and amenity standards.
- ix)  Manage residential development in a way that embraces innovative design and contemporary lifestyles.
- Ensure more certain outcomes for applicants, neighbours and the community.
In the case of any inconsistency between the controls in Part 5, the controls in Section B will prevail to the extent of the inconsistency.

## Objectives

- 1 To ensure dual occupancy development contributes to the greater Ku-ringgai landscape character of buildings within a landscaped garden setting including tall trees.
- 2 To ensure dual occupancy development conserves and enhances the visual character of the street with particular reference to integration of:
- built form and architecture,
- ii) building scale and setbacks;
- iii) fencing styles; and
- iv) landscaping and trees in gardens and on the public domain.
- 3 To ensure development makes a positive contribution to the public domain and all areas shared by the community.
- 4 To ensure the visual, scenic and environmental qualities on visually prominent sites are maintained by new development on or in the vicinity of prominent sites.
- 5 To reduce vehicle and driveway dominance and detraction from the prevailing Ku-ring-gai garden and canopy tree character

## Controls


## Visual Character

- 1 Design components of new development are to be based on the existing predominant and high quality visual character of the local neighbourhood. The local visual character is to be maintained by considering the following elements:
- visibility of the dual occupancy development when viewed from the street, public reserves and adjacent properties and how it integrates into and contributes to the local character;
- ii) relationship to the scale, layout and character of the tree dominated streetscape of Ku-ring-gai including canopy tree provisions within front gardens and on street verges;
- iii) retention and enhancement of features that contribute to Heritage Conservation Area character; and
- iv) front fencing to the street and public domain is to be consistent with the prevailing character of the street (see Section 5C.8: Fencing).
- 2 The prominent and high quality characteristics of the neighbourhood are to be identified and considered in Part 2 Site Analysis including reference to Part 14 Local Character Area and, where relevant, the Heritage Conservation Area and any biodiversity and environmental values.
Note: Visual character or streetscape is created by many features including: lot sizes, fencing, kerbs, setbacks, building separation and spaces between buildings, separation, access arrangements, street tree planting, tall tree canopy backdrop to the horizon, native vegetation and private gardens, as well the architecture of individual residences and their associated structures.

![page 4 img 2 (668x116)](images/ku-ring-gai-development-control-plan/p0001-05cd11004de3.png)


<!-- SRC: 08-part-5-dual-occupancy.pdf | PAGE: 5 -->

![page 5 img 1 (810x209)](images/ku-ring-gai-development-control-plan/p0001-1f61bd4b81b4.png)


## 5A.1 LOCAL CHARACTER AND STREETSCAPE (continued)


## Controls


## Public Domain and Urban Character

- 3 Development is to integrate with surrounding sites by:
- being of a scale consistent with the neighbourhood when viewed from the street, public domain or adjoining development;
- ii) not exceeding a two storey appearance to the street and to all adjacent sites including neighbouring development and public domain;
- iii) having a single storey presentation to the street in a Heritage Conservation Area or adjacent to a Heritage Item in order to be visually consistent with the height and scale of surrounding dwellings. In a two-storey streetscape in a Heritage Conservation Area two-storeys may be considered provided there is demonstrated integration with the existing character.
- iv) integrating built form and soft landscaping (gardens and trees) with the tree canopy that links the public and private domain throughout Ku-ring-gai.

## Visually Prominent Sites

- 4 Development on visually prominent sites is to:
- be integrated into the existing landscape through the site analysis and design process to minimise its visual dominance;
- ii) have a selection of external colours and finishes that are sensitive to the site and integrate into the locality;
- iii) retain existing landscape and vegetation elements;
- iv) consider views to the site and from the site; and
- embed the built form into the landscape by including tall trees and shrubs that form a setting for the building.
Note: Refer to dictionary for definition of visually prominent sites.

## 5A.2 SITE LAYOUT


## Further controls that may apply:

| SECTION A PART 13 - Tree and Vegetation Preservation   | SECTION B PART 19 -  Heritage items and Heritage Conservation Areas   | SECTION C PART 21 - General Site Design   |

## Objectives

- 1 To ensure attached dual occupancy dwellings are joined together by a common wall with no gap between the two dwellings
- 2 To maintain street surveillance and safety within and outside the development site.
- 3 To ensure dual occupancy development addresses the public domain including the street, any adjacent parks, reserves, walkways, public places.
- 4 To ensure the configuration of the dual occupancy development delivers good amenity to both dual occupancy dwellings and adjoining developments.
- 5 To discourage the use of Front-Back dual occupancy dwellings sites unless they deliver a clear planning benefit, including:
- retention of existing dwellings;
- maintenance of existing and original streetscape built form scale of large single dwellings within a garden setting, including tall canopy trees;
- protection of mature, vegetation or site features;
- conservation of heritage fabric and garden settings;

## Controls


## Dwelling Layout and Street Frontage

- 1 Dual occupancy dwellings can be either attached to each other or detached from each other. Attached dual occupancy dwellings are to have a common wall. If the dual occupancy does not have a common wall, it is detached and the building separation and setback controls apply. Common walls between garages only qualify if each of the garages is attached to the respective dwelling and its habitable rooms.
- 2 Dual occupancy dwellings are to be configured as follows (refer to Figure 5A.2-1):
- Side-Side: both dwellings are to face a public road; or,
- ii) Front-Back: one dwelling is to face a public road and the second dwelling located behind it; or,
- iii) Parallel Road: each dwelling is to face a public road, each with frontage to a different street/lane; or
- iv) Corner: each dwelling is to face a public road, one dwelling is to face the primary street, the second dwelling is to face the secondary street; or
- Battle-Axe: neither dwelling faces a public road and both are accessed from the street by a single driveway within an access handle.
- 3 The Front-Back layout will only be permitted where:
- the existing dwelling facing the street is retained or replaced with a significantly improved architectural building that maintains the scale of the existing dwelling, neighbouring homes, assimilates into and contributes to the streetscape;
- ii) it retains existing trees and landscape features (such as rock outcrops and established gardens);
- iii) it integrates into aHeritage Conservation Area, or assimilates with an adjacent Heritage Conservation Area or Heritage Item.
- 4 Battle-Axe layouts are discouraged and will only be permitted where they meet all the requirements of Part 5, including but not limited to provisions for landscaping, deep soil, tree planting, private open space, built upon area, setbacks and building separation.

## Lot Width

- 5 The Parent Lot is to have a minimum width at the street front building line as follows

- 6 Orient dwellings to a street frontage to provide active frontages, natural surveillance and clear, identifiable entries.
- 7 Provide site layouts that support practical pedestrian and vehicle access, with safe and efficient movement.
- 8 Respond to the opportunities and constraints of each site, including corner lots, secondary road access, and existing natural or built features.
- 9 To appropriately balance soft landscaping with built form.
- 10 To ensure lot widths enable built form within landscaped garden settings including tall trees, and avoid driveway dominance.

Dwelling Layout within a Heritage Conservation Area or Vicinity of HCA or Heritage Item

- 6 The Side-Side layout is not permitted within a Heritage Conservation Area.
- 7 The dual occupancy layout within a Heritage Conservation Area is to comply with the following:
- Retain the existing dwelling facing the street where it is a Contributory Item.
- ii) Retain existing trees and landscape features (such as rock outcrops, gardens and fencing).
- iii) Conserve building elements and garden settings that contribute to the character of a Heritage Conservation Area or the setting of an adjacent Heritage Item.

## 5A.3 BUILDING SETBACKS

## Objectives

- 1 To ensure setbacks minimise overlooking and overshadowing, maintain privacy, and preserve the visual and acoustic amenity of adjoining properties.
- 2 To ensure setbacks are dominated by landscaped gardens including tall shrubs and trees.
- 3 To enhance the retention of existing trees and vegetation.
- 4 To provide sufficient area for additional trees and landscaping to establish and grow to maturity.
- 5 To enable solar access and ventilation into the dual occupancy dwellings and solar access to their private open spaces.

## Front Setback

- 6 To provide front setbacks that support high quality landscaped front gardens that maintain the Kuring-gai character of built form in a garden setting including canopy trees.
- 7 To ensure setbacks maintain the established rhythm of the street, enhance the streetscape, and respond appropriately to any heritage settings.

## Controls


## Setbacks for all Layouts

- 1 The dual occupancy is to demonstrate consideration of:
- the existing setback of adjoining properties;
- ii) the setback pattern of its street block; and,
- iii) Council's minimum setback requirements.
- 2 Basement areas are to be fully consolidated under the building footprint and meet all setback requirements for each dwelling layout type as stated in this Part.
- 3 Reduced street front setbacks may be considered on the low side of the street where gradients, averaged over the front setback, exceed 20 degrees.
- 4 Side setbacks are to accommodate a pathway of maximum 0.9m and at least 0.6m of landscaping width to the side boundary for single storey buildings, and 1.1m for two storey buildings.
- 5 All side setbacks are to accommodate shrubs to a height of 2-3m for one storey dwellings and shrubs to a height of 3-4m for two storey dwellings.

## Side-Side Dwelling Layout


## Front Setback:

- 6 The front setback at the building line for each dual occupancy dwelling is to be a minimum of 12m.

## Rear Setback:

## 5A.4 BUILT-UPON AREA


## Further controls that may apply:

| SECTION A PART 1B.1 - Definitions   | SECTION B PART 15 - Land Contamination   | SECTION C PART 24 -  Water Management   |
|-------------------------------------|------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------|


## Objectives

- 1 To ensure dual occupancy development is consistent with the local built form and landscape character.
- 2 To provide sufficient soft landscaped area and deep soil for the retention and planting of tall trees and gardens with mature shrubbery.
- 3 To retain areas for habitat, connectivity and locally occurring native vegetation.
- 4 To enable planting around and between buildings to retain the Ku-ring-gai character of built form within a landscaped garden setting including canopy trees.
- 5 To minimise impervious surfaces and manage stormwater runoff.
- 6 To provide areas of usable, high-quality private open space.

## Controls

- 1 The maximum built upon area (BUA) requirements for all dual occupancy development sites is as follows
- 2 The front setback (measured as an area between the front boundary and front building line) for all dual occupancy development is to have a maximum BUA as follows (refer to figure 5A.4-3 to 5A.4-6)
| Parent Lot area       | Maximum BUA for each dual occupancy dwelling site   |
|-----------------------|-----------------------------------------------------|
| 1,015sqm - 1,249sqm   | 55%                                                 |
| 1,250sqm - 1,499sqm   | 52%                                                 |
| Greater than 1,500sqm | 50%                                                 |

| Dwelling layout                                  | Maximum BUA in front setback   |
|--------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------|
| Side-Side                                        | 50%                            |
| Front-Back                                       | 30%                            |
| Parallel Road Site                               | 30%                            |
| Corner Site - primary street frontage dwelling   | 40%                            |
| Corner Site - secondary street frontage dwelling | 40%                            |

Note: Applicants should make reasonable provisions for built elements such as pathways normally associated with a residential property as part of the built upon area. Council will also include elevated pathways as structures and built upon areas.

## 5A.5 LANDSCAPING

| Further controls that may apply:                      | Further controls that may apply:                                                                                                                                                                                                  | Further controls that may apply:                                                                      |

## Objectives

- 1 To retain and enhance existing tree canopy and ensure new planting contributes to the longterm tree canopy and landscaped character of the Ku-ring-gai area.
- 2 To ensure landscaping supports biodiversity and wildlife movement.
- 3 To ensure landscaped areas provide deep soil for tree growth and permeability for effective stormwater management.
- 4 To ensure landscaping, particularly in front gardens and setbacks, reduce building bulk, improve privacy and contribute to streetscape quality.
- 5 To provide landscaped areas that can support planting and that are usable for gardening and leisure activity.
- 6 To maintain the predominant garden setting of Ku-ring-gai streetscapes.

## Controls


## Landscaped Areas

- 1 The Parent Lot is to provide a minimum landscaped area equal to 50% of the Parent Lot area minus 100sqm. Each dwelling in a dual occupancy is to equally divide and include half of the required total landscaped area.
- 2 Landscaped areas are to have minimum dimension of 1.5m.
- 3 A minimum of 30% of each dual occupancy dwelling site is to be provided as deep soil area suitable for tall tree planting with a minimum dimension of 2m.
- 4 Gardens are to be designed to provide opportunities for green corridors and biodiversity connectivity, particularly where adjoining other landscaped or vegetated areas.
- 5 Landscaping forward of the building line is to present as a garden setting for the building, contribute to the landscape character of the streetscape, and to the continuity of front garden and tree canopy character within low density residential areas.
- 6 Side setbacks are to accommodate a path of maximum 0.9m and at least 0.6m of landscaping width to the side boundary for single storey buildings and1.1m for 2-storey buildings.

## Tree and landscape retention

- 7 Landscape proposals are to retain existing trees, particularly those located along boundaries or contributing to the streetscape character. This may be achieved by:
- minimising changes to existing ground levels within Notional Root Zones; and
- ii) confining building works to pre-existing building footprints where appropriate.
- 8 Natural landscape features, including trees and rock outcrops, are to be retained.
- 9 Location of driveways are to enable retention of street trees. Where

## 5B.1 VEHICLE ACCESS


## Further controls that may apply:

## Objectives

- 1 To reduce conflict with street and pedestrian traffic and optimise safety of both vehicular and pedestrian movement.
- 2 To create driveways that
- minimise hard surface runoff from the site;
- ii) are not visually intrusive on the existing streetscape;
- iii) have minimal impact on existing trees on site and the public domain;
- iv) do not dominate the street frontage nor have adverse impacts on street trees and on-site landscaping;
- are screened from neighbouring properties.
- 3 To avoid excavation and alteration of existing ground levels.
- 4 To reduce hard surfaces that contribute to urban heat island effects.
- 5 To ensure the number of driveway crossovers are minimised to prevent the cumulative visual and environmental impact of multiple dual occupancy developments within the street.
![page 24 img 2 (668x116)](images/ku-ring-gai-development-control-plan/p0001-05cd11004de3.png)


## Controls


## Vehicular Access

- 1 Driveways are to be located to ensure clear sight lines for both drivers and pedestrians.
- 2 The driveway is to be designed so that vehicles exit the property in a forward direction only where
- the access is located on a major roadway;
- ii) sight lines are restricted (such as at curves or crests);
- iii) the driveways are steep; or
- iv) driveways include access handles.

## Driveways

- 3 Driveway location and construction are to avoid adverse impacts on existing trees within the site and on the street verge, including to their Notional Root Zones.
- 4 The maximum crossing width for any driveway, as measured at the front site boundary, is to be
- 3.0m for all driveways into all dwelling layouts; or
- ii) 3.5m where a single driveway on the Parent Lot is provided to Side-Side dual occupancies as illustrated in Figure 5B.1-1.
- 5 A narrower width may be considered where trees are adversely affected.
- 6 The number of driveway crossings to the street are to be as follows
- Not more than one driveway is to be provided on any Parent Lot with a street frontage width of less than 18m.
- ii) A maximum of two driveways may be provided on Parent Lots with a street frontage wider than 18m, subject to site layout and tree protection.
- iii) The distance between the two driveway crossings at the street is to be a minimum 12m as illustrated in Figure 5B.1-1.
- iv) Where the minimum 12m distance cannot be achieved, the driveways are to be consolidated into a shared crossover, to reduce hard surfaces and visual dominance of driveways.
- A maximum of two driveways one per street frontage, are to be provided on Parent Lots on Corner Sites.

![page 25 img 1 (810x209)](images/ku-ring-gai-development-control-plan/p0001-1f61bd4b81b4.png)


## Objectives

- 6 To ensure driveway crossings do not impact neighbouring dwellings and do not prevent
- retention and planting of tall canopy trees on the street verge;
- ii) street parking for visitor cars and service vehicles directly in front of the dual occupancy development.
- iii) delivery of deep soil and landscaping, including canopy trees, within the front setback.
- 7 To ensure the development provides suitable and adequate collection space for Councils waste service including bins and bulky waste.

## Controls

- 7 Driveways are to be designed to minimise stormwater runoff through measures such as:
- porous paving;
- ii) directing runoff into landscaped garden areas; or
- iii) incorporating planting strips down the centre of the driveway.
- 8 A second driveway to existing street facing dwellings in a FrontBack layout may be considered where the driveway currently exists, and a 12m separation distance between the two driveways can be provided as illustrated in Figure 5B.1-2.

- 10 Only one driveway of maximum 3m width is to be provided for access to a dual occupancy battleaxe site.
- 11 Battleaxe layouts and Front-Back layouts are to specify any right of way driveway access into the rearmost dual occupancy dwelling.
- 12 A 0.6m minimum landscaped area is to be provided
- between the driveway and any side boundary; and
- ii) to any other boundary adjacent to the driveway.
- 13 Internal driveway design is to comply with AS 2890.1 Off Street Car Parking .

## Objectives

- 1 To encourage the provision of functional car parking facilities.
- 2 To minimise adverse visual and environmental impacts on the streetscape.
- 3 To ensure car spaces are of sufficient size to accommodate a standard vehicle.

## 5B.2 CAR PARKING PROVISION


## Controls

- 1 The number of on-site parking spaces provided are to be in accordance with Section C Part 22R of this DCP.
- 2 Internal access to car parking and the required car parking area is to be no greater than 31sqm per dwelling. Car parking and access to that car parking, exceeding the requirements of this control will not be excluded from the gross floor area as defined in KLEP 2015.
- 3 The minimum dimensions of a residential parking space are to be as illustrated in Figure 5B2.1.

## 5B.3 CARPORTS AND GARAGES

## Objectives


## Controls

- 1 To ensure carports and garages
- do not dominate the appearance of the dwelling;
- ii) present as complementary visual elements within the streetscape; and
- iii) are not the primary built form when viewing the dwelling from the street or public domain.
- 2 To encourage the design of functional car parking facilities that are integrated with the built form of each dwelling.
- 3 To ensure the location of carports and garages considers existing trees and structures on adjacent sites, streetscape and visual character.
- 4 To minimise impacts of excavation on the built environment and the streetscape.
- 5 To avoid excavation in the front setback area and maintain existing ground levels to the street.

## Design of Carports and Garages

- 1 Garages and carports are to be set back a minimum of 1m behind the building line at the front setback to the street.
- 2 Garages and carports as a percentage of the total dwelling facade is not to exceed the maximum percentages specified in the following table
| Dwelling layout     | Parent Lot width   | Garaging as a percentage of the total facade   |
|---------------------|--------------------|------------------------------------------------|
| Side-Side           | 18m* - 21m         | 50%                                            |
|                     | greater than 22m   | 40%                                            |
| Front-Back          | greater than 25m   | 40%                                            |
| Parallel roads      | 15m - 20m          | 40%                                            |
|                     | greater than 21m   | 30%                                            |
| Corner (short side) | 15 - 25m           | 40%                                            |
|                     | greater than 25m   | 30%                                            |
| Corner (long side)  | All                | 30%                                            |

Note: * Lots with a Parent Lot width of less than 18m in a side by side typology will be subject to merit based assessment, having regard to the extent to which the design minimises car dominance within the streetscape.

## 5B.3 CARPORTS AND GARAGES (continued)


## Controls

- 3 The scale and design of carport and garage structures are:
- to be sympathetic to existing development on-site;
- ii) to consider adjacent buildings;
- iii) to be integrated into the building design; and
- iv) not to dominate the site, dwelling elevation, landscape, or the streetscape.
- 4 Basement garages are only permitted on sloping land and where no more than 1m excavation is required for driveway access.

## Location of Parking Structures

- 5 Location of all garages and driveways are to enable preservation of existing site and street trees.

## Detached Carports and Garages

- 6 Detached garages are to be single storey and set back 1.5m minimum from side and rear boundaries.
- 7 Detached carports are to be single storey and set back 0.6m minimum from side and rear boundaries.
Note: Where there is any inconsistency between this Part and Part 22 of this DCP in relation to vehicular access, car parking or garages, this section prevails to the extent of the inconsistency.

## 5C.1 BUILDING ENVELOPES


## Objectives


## Controls

- 1 To maintain a twostorey domestic scale to ensure dual occupancies are consistent with the surrounding low-density residential character.
- 2 To ensure the bulk and scale of buildings are proportionate to lot size and compatible with the established residential character of the locality.
- 3 To reinforce the established rhythm and character of the streetscape through building form, siting and landscaping.
- 4 To protect significant bushland, distant views and the broader landscape setting.
- 5 To minimise overshadowing, overlooking and visual intrusion on the private open space, solar access and outlook of adjoining properties.

## Basements

- 6 To minimise basements and excavation so that development follows existing ground levels.
- 7 To prevent excavation outside the building footprint and ensure deep soil provision that supports retention and growth of canopy trees.
- 8 To prevent a three-storey appearance to the street, and other public domain including adjacent parks, reserves, walkways, public places, and to neighbouring sites.

## Height

- 1 The maximum height of each dual occupancy dwelling is 9.5m (including any garage, basement or similar) and present as
- no more than two-storeys above natural ground level from the street and adjoining properties; or
- ii) in an HCA or in the vicinity of an HCA or Heritage Item, present as no more than a single storey plus first floor in the roof from the street and adjoining properties.
Note: Standards (in metres) for the external height of the building are set within KLEP 2015.

![page 32 img 2 (668x116)](images/ku-ring-gai-development-control-plan/p0001-05cd11004de3.png)


*Figure 5C.1-1: Maximum height of buildings*

- 2 Development is to avoid the creation of an overbearing effect upon neighbouring dwellings by ensuring all built structures are within the building height plane as illustrated in Figure 5C.1-2.
- 3 The bulk and scale of dual occupancy dwellings are to demonstrate consideration of impacts on neighbouring properties and local character including:
- overlooking and overshadowing of living and private open space areas and solar panels;
- ii) adverse impacts on any bushland or distant views; and
- iii) the relationship with the streetscape.

## Basements

- 4 Basements are not permitted. Only basement garages on steeply sloping sites may be considered.
- 5 Where basement parking demonstrates a maximum 1m excavation, it is to be
- consolidated directly under the building footprint;
- ii) limited to garage area only, no habitable nor other spaces are permitted;
- iii) include a maximum ceiling height of 2.2m.
- 6 With the exception of steeply sloping sites, avoid excavation in the front setback area and maintain existing ground levels to the street.

## Slope and Topography

- 7 Site planning and dwelling design is to minimise cut and fill excavation works. Development is to follow the natural groundline and dwellings are to be stepped to accommodate steep sites.

## 5C.2 BUILDING FACADES


## Further controls that may apply:

SECTION B

PART 20 -  Development Near Road or Rail Noise


## Controls


## Street Frontages

- 1 Extensive blank or unarticulated walls to street frontages are not permitted.
- 2 All external facades are to be articulated to reduce building mass and present a human scale. This may be achieved through the use of window openings, window awnings, verandas, entry porches, staggered wall planes, a combination of materials and finishes, decorative architectural elements including brick corbelling banding, and hipped/gabled roofs.
- 3 Except where the dual occupancies have been designed to present as one big home to the street frontage, each dual occupancy dwelling is to incorporate a variation in entry design, façade articulation, and materials to distinguish each dwelling and avoid a monotonous appearance. Identical or repetitious façades facing the same street frontage will not be permitted.
- 4 External walls, including to side boundaries, are to be modulated to reduce bulk and scale by incorporating bays, recesses or courtyards.
- 5 The maximum length of any unmodulated wall is 12m, or 8m where walls exceed 4m in height.
![page 34 img 2 (668x116)](images/ku-ring-gai-development-control-plan/p0001-05cd11004de3.png)


*Figure 5C.2-1: Dual occupancy dwellings with modulation and articulation.*


## Objectives

- 1 To encourage well designed, attractive and site responsive buildings.
- 2 To minimise the bulk and scale of the built form.
- 3 To ensure built form contributes positively to the street and public domain by providing active street frontages, and reinforcing the rhythm and character of the street.
- 4 To ensure dual occupancy development respects established residential patterns by maintaining street-oriented dwellings, landscaped front gardens, and usable rear yards.
- 5 To ensure building orientation addresses the street and provides natural surveillance, and clear, identifiable entries.
- 6 To ensure high impact elements such as noise sources are considered early in the design stage.
- 7 Façade design is to achieve a cohesive and contemporary character, using materials and architectural elements in a way that creates visual interest and reinforces human scale.
SECTION C

PART 23.3 -  Sustainability of Building Materials

## Objectives

- 8 Visual clutter and unauthentic reproduction styles are to be avoided, including applied decorative features or faux heritage detailing that are not integral to the building form.
- 9 To ensure front entries are clearly identifiable elements of the façade, contributing to human scale and the dwelling's relationship with the street.
- 10 To ensure dual occupancy development within a Heritage Conservation Area or adjacent to a Heritage Item integrates and contributes to the local prevailing character.

## 5C.2 BUILDING FACADES (continued)


## Controls


## Articulation

- 6 Articulation of building facades is to complement modulation and may include windows, porches, verandahs, shading devices, and materials/finishes.
- 7 Façades are to be articulated to provide interest but avoid excessive detailing that results in a cluttered or disorderly appearance.
- 8 Materials and colours are to be simple and cohesive, with no more than four used on any elevation.
- 9 Applied or decorative features that are not integral to the building's structure (such as screens, trims or panels) may be used as secondary elements but are not a substitute for modulation or genuine articulation of the building form. Where used, such features must be integrated into the overall design.
- 10 Building facades are to be designed in a contemporary manner consistent with the established residential character. Pastiche or reproduction styles (such as applied heritage detailing or faux historic features) are not permitted.
- 11 Modifications to an existing street facing dwelling being altered to accommodate two dual occupancy dwellings are to be:
- designed so that they are integrated into and improve the existing building appearance;
- ii) result in the new and old structures appearing as one building from the street. This may be achieved through the choice of materials, detailing, building proportion and configuration.
- 12 Building design is to integrate soft landscaping and natural site features and make provision for tall shrub planting.
- 13 Where dwellings are located near a busy road or railway line, the requirements of Part 20.1 of this DCP are to be included.
- 14 Dwellings facing the street are to have clearly visible front doors. Porticos to front doors are to be single storey.

## 5C.2 BUILDING FACADES (continued)


## Controls


## Corner Sites

- 15 Corner sites must address both street frontages with appropriate windows, articulation and landscaping as illustrated in Figure 5C.2-2.

![page 37 img 1 (810x209)](images/ku-ring-gai-development-control-plan/p0001-1f61bd4b81b4.png)


## Objectives

- 1 To ensure first floor and roof forms present as a domestic two-storey scale consistent with Ku-ringgai's low-density housing character.
- 2 To avoid an overbearing bulk and scale relationship with neighbouring properties, particularly on sloping sites.
- 3 To design facades to minimise overlooking from first floor windows and respect the amenity of neighbouring dwellings and private open space.
- 4 To ensure roof forms contribute positively to the overall dwelling design and streetscape character without dominating the building or locality.
- 5 To ensure rooms are of sufficient size and proportion to allow for practical furniture placement and effective use of space.
- 6 To ensure living areas relate directly to private open space, supporting natural light, ventilation, and outdoor living.
- 7 To ensure the dual occupancy dwellings provide separate entries and internal layouts that maintain visual and acoustic privacy and amenity between dwellings.

## 5C.3 DWELLING DESIGN AND LAYOUT


## Controls

- 1 Each dual occupancy dwelling is to meet all of the following standards
- minimum width of 6.5m;
- ii) the kitchen is not to form part of a circulation space such as a hallway;
- iii) the principal living room is to have a minimum internal dimension of 4m;
- iv) bedrooms are to have a minimum dimension of 3m, excluding space for wardrobes;
- windows and doors to habitable rooms are preferably to be oriented to the front and rear of the site;
- vi) each dwelling is to be provided with a clearly identifiable and separate entry with clear and safe access;
- vii) windows from habitable rooms are to overlook the public domain to provide passive surveillance; and
- viii) where the side of a dwelling faces a secondary street, the façade is to incorporate windows and other articulation to positively address the street.
- 2 The dwelling orientation and internal layout is to avoid direct overlooking between the two dual occupancy dwellings (e.g. living areas facing each other at close range).
- 3 All detached dual occupancies are to provide fencing between the dwellings in line with setback requirements and subdivision plans.
- 4 All dual occupancy dwellings are to be of Silver Level as indicated in the Livable Housing Design Guidelines and the National Construction Code accessibility requirements regardless of site steepness.

## Roof Form

- 5 Roof forms are to be designed to minimise bulk and overshadowing of neighbouring buildings and open spaces.
- 6 Roof forms are to be integrated into the dwelling design and be consistent with the established streetscape character.
- 7 Gables, dormers, clerestories and other roof elements are to remain subordinate to the overall roof form and not add excessive bulk or visual dominance.
- 8 Dual Occupancies in Heritage Conservation Areas or in the vicinity of HCAs or Heritage Items are to provide hip and gabled roof forms. Flat roofs are not permitted.

## Objectives

- 8 To deliver dwellings able to accommodate people of all ages and abilities, supporting ageing in place and housing choice.

## 5C.3 DWELLING DESIGN AND LAYOUT (continued)


## Controls


## Attic Rooms and Dormer Windows

- 9 Attic rooms above the ground floor are encouraged in areas with a predominantly single storey character above the ground floor level.
- 10 Attic rooms within the roof space above the first floor level will not be permitted.
- 11 Dormer windows to attic rooms are to be located and have a size, bulk and scale that do not dominate the roof form or add excessively to the bulk of the building.
Note: Where a dormer window provides the primary source for required solar access and/or daylight to a habitable room, it is to be of a size that provides adequate natural daylight to all parts of a habitable room, and the required solar access if for a living room.

- 12 Unless otherwise consistent with the form of development within the immediate locality, the configuration of dormer windows must satisfy the following:
- be positioned a minimum of 0.2m below the main roof ridge height;
- ii) not to extend beyond the external wall of the dwelling; and
- iii) be set back from the sides of the roof by a minimum of 0.5m.
- 13 Dormers occurring in the same roof plane must be similarly sized and configured, and arranged symmetrically.
- 14 The location, size, configuration and layout of clerestory windows and skylights must be sympathetic to the overall design of the dwelling and the streetscape.

## 5C.4 PRIVATE OPEN SPACE


## Further controls that may apply:


## Objectives

- 1 To ensure each dual occupancy dwelling provides functional private open space that is easily accessed from habitable rooms to support everyday outdoor living.

## Controls

- 1 A minimum principal private open space of 25.0sqm is to be provided to each dual occupancy dwelling, as in Figure 4C.4-1. The private open space is to:
- have a minimum internal dimension of 4.0m;
- ii) have direct level access from the living/dining area;
- iii) be located behind the building line;
- iv) provide a consolidated paved area of 12.0sqm and a minimum width of 3.0m; and
- accommodate a table and 6 chairs directly accessible from the living/dining area with no obstructions including stairs;
Note: Access from living/dining rooms is to have no obstructions including stairs.

Note: A step at the threshold for compliance with waterproofing requirements is acceptable.

- 2 The principal private open space is to be oriented to the north, east or west wherever possible to receive daily solar access.
- 3 All private open space area requirements are exclusive of any areas for the provision of services such as fixed drying areas.

## Objectives

- 1 To ensure the design and siting of new development maintains daylight and sunlight to habitable rooms, private open space, and solar collectors of
- new dual occupancy dwellings;
- ii) existing dwellings converted into dual occupancy dwellings; and
- iii) neighbouring dwellings.

## 5C.5 SOLAR ACCESS


## Controls

|   1 | Each dual occupancy dwelling is to receive a minimum 3 hours of direct sunlight between 9am and 3pm on 21 June to a north-facing window to a main living area (living room, rumpus, lounge, dining), and to the principal private open space.                                              |
|-----|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
|   2 | All habitable rooms are to have a window in an external wall that is directly visible from every part of the room. Snorkel windows are not permitted.                                                                                                                                      |
|     | Note: Refer to Part 1B.1 for definition of snorkel window.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|   3 | The use of lightwells, skylight, or high level windows as a primary source of daylight in habitable rooms is not permitted.                                                                                                                                                                |
|   4 | Dual occupancy development is to be designed and sited to maintain solar access to adjoining properties for at least 3 hours between 9am and 3pm on 21 June to north facing windows of habitable rooms (excluding windows facing side boundaries) and to the principal private open space. |
|   5 | Where existing overshadowing from buildings or topography makes 1 and 2 above unachievable, development must not further reduce sunlight by more than 20% in time or area.                                                                                                                 |
|   6 | Development is to consider the use of sun protection devices that preserve internal amenity. These can include window shades and awnings, roof and eave overhangs, use of pergolas and landscaping for shading of openings.                                                                |
|     | Note : Avoid the use of dark tinted glazing as this impacts on streetscape character and internal amenity for daylight., beneficial solar access and outlook.                                                                                                                              |
|   7 | Professionally prepared shadow diagrams must accompany all applications for dual occupancies exceeding one storey. Refer to Council's DA guide available on Council's website. https://www.krg. nsw.gov.au.                                                                                |
